chapters.title: Chapter 2: Crude Oil and the Global Economy

lessons.title: Investing Around Oil: OMCs, Upstream Plays, and Oil ETFs

children.text: Every Way to Invest Around Oil Comes With Baggage

You cannot buy a barrel of crude through your regular demat account. What you can buy is a company, or a fund, whose fortunes move with the barrel, and every single option carries baggage that the barrel itself does not: government policy, refining economics, and in the one case where a real oil ETF exists, a structural cost of simply holding the fund. This lesson goes through the three practical routes, upstream producers, oil marketing companies, and the honest answer on ETFs, and shows why none of them is a clean, one-to-one bet on the crude oil cycle.

body.text: There is no pure oil price stock in India. Every listed proxy adds either government policy risk, refining economics, or fund structure cost on top of the commodity bet.

children.text: Upstream Plays: ONGC and Oil India

ONGC and Oil India actually pump crude out of the ground, which should make them the closest thing to a direct bet on the oil price. In practice, the government has repeatedly stepped in to capture part of the upside during price spikes, which means a rising crude price does not flow through to their earnings as cleanly as it looks on the surface.

body.text: In July 2022, faced with a surge in international crude prices and unusually high refining margins on fuel exports, the government introduced a windfall profit tax, technically a Special Additional Excise Duty on domestically produced crude and on exports of diesel, petrol and aviation turbine fuel, revised roughly every two weeks in line with global prices. This tax was withdrawn in 2024. Policies like this get introduced and removed based on government decisions, so verify the current status before assuming any historical rule still applies.

body.caption: Upstream Producers: What Actually Drives the Stock

cells: Higher global prices lift revenue per barrel produced, before any government levy
Can cap how much of a price spike actually reaches profit, and has changed materially over the past decade
Ageing fields and execution delays on new projects matter as much as price, and are entirely company-specific
As majority government-owned entities, capital allocation and dividend policy are influenced by the government's own fiscal needs, not purely business logic

children.text: Oil Marketing Companies: Two Businesses in One Stock

IOC, BPCL and HPCL are often assumed to simply lose when crude rises, because they buy crude and sell fuel. That is only half the picture. Each of these companies also runs refineries, and a refiner's profit depends on the gross refining margin, the spread between the value of the refined products it sells and the cost of the crude it processes, which can move independently of the crude price's direction entirely.

body.label: Gross Refining Margin (GRM)
body.value: Value of refined products minus cost of crude processed
body.context: Usually quoted in dollars per barrel. A refiner can post a strong quarter even in a falling crude price environment if refining margins are wide, and a weak quarter in a rising price environment if margins are thin.

children.text: On top of the refining business, OMCs also earn a marketing margin on every litre sold at the pump. Under India's daily dynamic pricing regime, this margin can get squeezed when crude spikes faster than retail prices are allowed to adjust, particularly if there is political pressure to hold pump prices steady. A third factor, inventory valuation, adds one more layer: OMCs hold physical stock of crude and fuel, so a rising price can create a one-off accounting gain on existing inventory, while a falling price creates a loss, independent of the ongoing refining or marketing business.

The Honest Answer on Oil ETFs

As Chapter 1 covered, there is no crude oil ETF listed on the NSE or BSE. If you want ETF-style exposure to crude specifically, the realistic route is a fund like the United States Oil Fund, listed in the US, accessible to Indian residents only by opening an international trading account under the RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, which caps how much money an individual can send abroad each year. This is a meaningfully more complex and costly route than buying a domestic ETF: it involves currency conversion, a separate account with its own fees, and exposure to US tax rules on the position.

body.text: Funds like the United States Oil Fund hold front-month crude futures rather than physical oil, and have to roll those contracts forward every month. When the futures curve is in contango, a normal state for oil discussed in Chapter 1, this roll happens at a loss, quietly eroding returns over time even if the spot oil price is roughly flat. This structural decay is a well documented, long-running criticism of oil futures ETFs and is a real cost, not a theoretical one.

body.title: Diagnose the Gap
body.scenario: Brent crude rises 20% over a quarter. ONGC's stock price rises only 5% over the same period, noticeably lagging the commodity move.
body.prompt: List at least two plausible, company-specific reasons for this gap that have nothing to do with crude oil demand or supply.
body.modelAnswer: Windfall tax or cess policy could be capturing a meaningful share of the incremental revenue from higher prices, so realised profit rises by far less than the headline crude price. Production volumes may be flat or declining due to ageing fields or project delays, meaning ONGC has less additional oil to sell at the higher price even before tax. The stock may also be pricing in government-ownership-related risks, such as an expected dividend payout that serves government fiscal needs rather than being reinvested, or market skepticism that the price gain is temporary. None of these reasons require crude oil fundamentals to explain the gap; they are all specific to ONGC as a company operating inside a policy environment.

points: Upstream producers like ONGC and Oil India look like a direct bet on crude, but government windfall tax and cess policy have historically capped how much of a price spike reaches their bottom line.

OMCs like IOC, BPCL and HPCL run two businesses at once, refining and marketing, and their stock performance depends on gross refining margins and inventory valuation gains as much as on the direction of the crude price itself.

There is no domestic oil ETF. Genuine ETF exposure to crude means accessing a US-listed fund via the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, which adds currency, account and structural roll-cost complexity that a domestic ETF investor never has to think about.

Every proxy for the oil cycle in an Indian portfolio comes with baggage that has nothing to do with the oil price itself. Reading the cycle correctly, as the earlier lessons in this chapter covered, is necessary but not sufficient; you also have to understand what you're actually buying.
